name: Jayden Southworth
intro: I build software, tools, and experiments around the problem at hand.
bio: My work spans personal tools, game mods, and web applications. I like turning a complicated problem into something clear to use and straightforward to maintain.
background: Alongside personal programming projects, I’ve worked in customer-facing, team leadership, and operations roles. That experience shapes how I think about the people on the other side of an interface.
educationDetail: Merit America’s 30-week full-stack development program, completed in 2022, covered Java, SQL and Spring, client-server programming, and React. Additional Front-End Web Development with React certificate through the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology on Coursera, 2022.

skills.name: Interface
skills.example: Store Shoppers uses server-rendered HTML and HTMX for catalog, basket, and manager interactions.

skills.name: Application
skills.example: My training projects included client-server request flows, program-state design, and refactoring larger functions into smaller methods.

skills.name: Data & workflow
skills.example: The projects here include database-backed application flows and file-based inventory and transaction logs.

projects.name: Vendo-Matic 800
projects.summary: A vending-machine flow from deposit to product selection and correct change.
projects.detail: A virtual vending machine with a command-line interface. Inventory is read from a text file, and transactions are logged back to a file.
projects.contribution: I worked on program-state design and refactored complex functions into smaller methods, making the transaction flow easier to follow.

notes.overview: Vendo-Matic 800 models a vending machine in a command-line application. It reads inventory from a text file and writes transactions to a log. The flow runs from a deposit and product selection through to change.

detail.title: From inventory to a transaction log
detail.body: The inventory enters through a text file; transactions are written to a log. Between those file operations, the program handles the deposit, product selection, and change. The refactoring work focused on breaking larger functions into smaller methods around that flow.

projects.name: TEnmo
projects.summary: Peer-to-peer transfer requests, approvals, and account interactions.
projects.detail: A command-line client communicates with a REST API so users can send, request, and approve money transfers. The backend uses Spring Data JPA and Spring Security.
projects.contribution: I worked on API request exchanges, server-side architecture, and the client-side connection logic that joins the flow together.

notes.overview: TEnmo uses a command-line client and a REST API to let users send, request, and approve money transfers. The backend uses Spring Data JPA and Spring Security, with PostgreSQL for data storage.

detail.title: Across the client-server boundary
detail.body: The command-line interface is the user’s entry point. Requests cross into the REST API, with PostgreSQL behind the application’s data.

projects.name: Store Shoppers
projects.summary: A local market, from basket to order.
projects.detail: A neighborhood-market demo connecting a searchable storefront and simulated checkout with manager inventory controls and an order queue.
projects.contribution: Storefront, inventory tools, and order workflow.
projects.status: Personal demo · Fake products and simulated orders. No payments or real fulfillment.

notes.overview: Store Shoppers is a neighborhood-market demo built with Go, HTMX and SQLite. A searchable catalog leads to a basket and simulated checkout; a manager workspace handles inventory adjustments and an order queue.

detail.title: Keeping the order and the shelves in sync
detail.body: One Go server renders HTML, with HTMX updating forms and page fragments. Checkout saves the order and deducts stock in one SQLite transaction. Repeat submissions return the existing order; inventory adjustments keep an audit trail, and fulfillment changes follow guarded transitions.

experiment.name: Aethel
experiment.summary: A structured-writing experiment built with SvelteKit, TypeScript and TipTap/ProseMirror. Explores object-reference chips, timeline state, undo/redo, browser persistence, and JSON import/export.

sections.title: References inside the text
sections.body: A custom TipTap extension turns a double-bracket reference into an inline chip. It stores the object’s identifier separately from the displayed text, along with its status and color. Clicking a resolved chip can open the referenced object.

sections.title: Reversible changes
sections.body: The editor’s history system supports undo and redo. Related operations can be grouped into one history entry; undo runs the group in reverse, and redo reapplies it in order.

sections.title: A project you can save
sections.body: The serialization layer gathers objects, timeline placements and timeslots, milestones, and interface state into a project file. Browser import and export use JSON, including the .aethel file extension. Import checks the expected project structure before restoring it.

originCaption: I like to write, and build things, sometimes.
origin: A lot of my coding has been personal work: modding games, fixing mods, and learning on my own.
My projects range from game mods and web applications to Aethel, a structured-writing prototype. I learn what the problem calls for and build from there.
